queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.
queries.act: Turn toward what lasts: serve, study, reflect daily, and offer your work to something beyond yourself.

hook.speaker: Krishna
hook.setting: Arjuna asks which way of devotion is best; Krishna promises what he does for those who turn to him.
hook.sanskrit: तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् । भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥
hook.line: Whoever rests their heart in me, I lift out of the drowning sea, and soon.
hook.translation: For those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Partha, I very soon become the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and endless change.

words.en: from the ocean of mortal existence
of those whose minds are fixed

alternates.speaker: Krishna
alternates.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
alternates.sanskrit: तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया । उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः ॥
alternates.line: Learn from those who have seen the truth: approach with humility, ask real questions, and serve.
alternates.translation: Learn it by bowing down, by questioning, and by service. Those who are wise and have seen the truth will teach you that knowledge.
alternates.why: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

prasang.title: The glory of knowledge
prasang.summary: Krishna praises knowledge: learn it humbly from those who know, it carries even the worst wrongdoer across, faith and self-control bring it, and doubt destroys. He ends: cut your doubt and stand up.
prasang.lesson: Learn humbly, trust the process, and cut through doubt to act.

alternates.speaker: Krishna
alternates.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
alternates.sanskrit: वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहायनवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि । तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
alternates.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
alternates.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
alternates.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.
alternates.misuse: Not a way to brush off someone else's grief with 'they've just changed clothes'.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks which way of devotion is best; Krishna promises what he does for those who turn to him.
verse.sanskrit: तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् । भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ॥
verse.line: Whoever rests their heart in me, I lift out of the drowning sea, and soon.
verse.translation: For those whose minds are absorbed in me, O Partha, I very soon become the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and endless change.

words.en: from the ocean of mortal existence
of those whose minds are fixed

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks which path of devotion is the best. Krishna answers that whoever rests their heart in him, he very soon becomes the one who lifts them out of the ocean of death and endless change.
verse.for_you: You are searching for what it is all for after losing a parent. The texts call this the ocean of endless change. Krishna offers to be the lifter, not the answer. You do not have to find the depth alone.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment of rest in the chaos, and let it be enough.
verse.scene_line: You are standing at the edge of the ocean, and the lifter is already reaching for you.
asks: How do I rest my heart when I am drowning in daily life?
What does it mean to rest my heart in something I cannot see?
Will the lifter lift me even if I do not know how to swim?

verse.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
verse.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
verse.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
verse.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
verse.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

verse.meaning: The narrator tells the reader about the self that lives in the heart. We meet it every night in deep sleep, but we do not know it is there. The text says that creatures pass into this world of Brahman daily, yet they do not find it. They are carried away by untruth, missing the treasure buried right beneath their feet, just as people walk over gold and never see it.
verse.for_you: You wake up, you go to work, you are with your family. You pass through deep sleep every night and meet something vast, but you do not know it. You are looking for what it is all for, and it is already under your feet.
verse.try_today: Notice the quiet moment before you fully wake up.
verse.scene_line: You are walking over buried gold in your own sleep.
asks: How do I know the treasure is really there?
What does it mean that I am carried away by untruth?
Can I find this world of Brahman without seeking?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: नैव प्रार्थयते लाभं नालाभेनानुशोचति । धीरस्य शीतलं चित्तममृतेनैव पूरितम् ॥
verse.line: Not begging for gain, not grieving loss: a steady mind stays cool and full.
verse.translation: He does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady one's cool mind is filled as if with nectar.
verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise. He tells Janaka that the one who does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss, holds a steady mind that stays cool and full as if with nectar. The point is that calm is not a prize to chase or a place to reach. It is simply how you hold ordinary life, right where you are, without needing the world to change first.
verse.for_you: You have been walking over buried gold for a while, and now the ground beneath your feet feels unsteady. The search for what it is all for has left you with very little time that is your own.
verse.try_today: Rest your heart in the steady ground of one ordinary task today.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own kitchen, holding a cup, and the ground beneath your feet is steady.
asks: How do I hold ordinary life without needing it to change first?
What does it mean to rest my heart in something steady?
Where is the steady ground beneath my feet right now?

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: The seer on where the Lord is found and how one comes to see him.
verse.sanskrit: अणोरणीयान् महतो महीयानात्मा गुहायां निहितोऽस्य जन्तोः । तमक्रतुः पश्यति वीतशोको धातुः प्रसादान्महिमानमीशम् ॥
verse.line: The Lord is hidden in your own heart. By his grace one sees him, and sorrow lifts.
verse.translation: Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the heart of every creature. One free of grasping sees him, the Lord in his greatness, by the grace of the Creator, and is free of sorrow.
verse.why: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.
verse.misuse: Grace here is not a reward for being good enough; the verse pairs it with letting go of grasping.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

verse.meaning: The Seer tells the Seekers that the Lord is hidden in their own heart. He is smaller than the small, yet greater than the great. A person free of grasping sees him by the grace of the Creator, and sorrow lifts. The verse proposes that true refuge is not found by running away from the question of what governs our lives, but by letting go of the tight hold on outcomes and allowing the hidden presence within to be seen.
verse.for_you: The grief and fear of death you carry are searching for a place to land. The text offers no quick fix, only the quiet possibility that the answer is already where you sit, beneath the noise of work and family.
verse.try_today: Notice the moment when the mind stops grasping and rests.
verse.scene_line: You are a seeker walking daily over the buried gold of your own heart.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the reader about how to live in the world. They have just said that everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. Now they say that you could do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. The point is that there is no other way to live than to work and let go. When you do your work in this spirit, your actions do not cling to you like a burden. You keep working, but you hold what you do lightly.
verse.for_you: You are working and raising your children, and you have lost a parent. The weight of it is there. The verse does not ask you to stop working or to detach from your family. It says to keep working, but to hold it lightly.
verse.try_today: Do one task at work or home without trying to control the result.
verse.scene_line: You are at the edge of your own buried gold, walking past it every day.
asks: How do I do my work without clinging to it?
What does it mean to hold my work lightly?
Can I wish for a long life and still let go?

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
verse.sanskrit: न चाभ्युदितसायी स्यात्प्रायश्चित्ती तथा भवेत् / मातापितरमुत्थाय पूर्वमेवाभिवादयेत् / आचार्यमथवाऽप्यन्तं तथाऽऽयुर्विदन्ते महत्
verse.line: Start the day by greeting your mother and father. Small daily respect adds up to a good life.
verse.translation: Don't sleep past sunrise. On rising, first greet your mother and father, and your teacher or another elder; that is how a long life is won.
verse.why: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

prasang.title: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

verse.meaning: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how a person lives long and well. Bhishma tells him that a good life is not built from grand deeds alone, but from small, daily conduct. He says do not sleep past sunrise. On rising, first greet your mother and father, and your teacher or another elder. That is how a long life is won. He adds that a steady mind stays cool and full when it is not begging for gain and not grieving loss.
verse.for_you: The searching you are living with is a search for what it is all for. You are carrying the weight of work and the children, and the grief of losing a parent. Bhishma says the foundation of a good life is small daily respect.
verse.try_today: When you wake, before checking your phone, look at your parents and say good morning.
verse.scene_line: You are standing in your own morning, asked how to live well.
asks: How does greeting them change the rest of my day?
What if I am not close to my parents anymore?

story.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
story.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.
story.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
story.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

anchor.speaker: Vasishtha
anchor.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha tells Rama how worry feeds itself.
anchor.sanskrit: चिन्तनेनैधते चिन्ता त्विन्धनेनेव पावकः । नश्यत्यचिन्ततेनैव विनेन्धनमिवानलः ॥
anchor.line: Worry grows when you feed it thought, like fire with fuel. Starve it, and it dies down.
anchor.translation: Worry grows by thinking, as fire grows with fuel; and it dies by not being thought, as fire dies without fuel.
anchor.why: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् । अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
verse.line: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.
verse.translation: I see nothing that could drive away this sorrow that is drying up my senses, not even an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth or rule over the gods.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna is on the battlefield. He has dropped his bow and his knees are shaking. He tells Krishna that even a kingdom of gold or rule over the gods would not stop the grief that is eating him from the inside. He admits he cannot see a way forward and asks Krishna to teach him what to do. The verse says that admitting you do not know where to turn and asking for help is the first step toward seeing clearly.
verse.for_you: The weight you carry does not come from a single bad day. It is the slow drying out of your own senses, the sense that nothing you have won or built will touch this. You have reached a place where you cannot tell the right choice from the wrong one.
verse.try_today: Notice the exact moment today when your mind goes quiet, and let that silence ask the question for you.
verse.scene_line: You stand on your own battlefield, bow in hand, and admit that even victory would not touch this grief.
asks: How do I tell the difference between grief and a dead end?
What does it mean to ask for help when I am used to carrying it alone?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: आदित्यस्य गतागतैरहरहः संक्षीयते जीवितं व्यापारैर्बहुकार्यभारगुरुभिः कालोऽपि न ज्ञायते । दृष्ट्वा जन्मजराविपत्तिमरणं त्रासश्च नोत्पद्यते पीत्वा मोहमयीं प्रमादमदिरामुन्मत्तभूतं जगत् ॥
verse.line: Each sunrise takes a day from us, and, busy with work, we never notice time slipping by.
verse.translation: With the sun's coming and going, life shrinks day by day; with business heavy with many tasks, we do not notice time passing; seeing birth, age, misfortune and death, we feel no alarm. The world has drunk the wine of heedlessness and gone mad.
verse.why: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader about the slipping of time. He says that with the sun's rising and setting, life shrinks day by day. He says that with work heavy and full of tasks, we do not notice time passing. He says that seeing birth, age, misfortune, and death, we feel no alarm. He says the world has drunk the wine of heedlessness and gone mad.
verse.for_you: You are busy with work and your family. The days move fast, and you do not notice them slipping by. The grief of losing your parent is still there. Notice the time that is passing, and let your hands rest from the tasks for a moment.
verse.try_today: Pause for one minute and feel the sun on your face.
verse.scene_line: You are busy with work while time slips by and death waits.
asks: What am I doing with the time I have left?
How do I notice time while I am busy?

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: After Sita is taken, Lakshman comforts Ram, who is lost in grief.
verse.sanskrit: आश्वसिही नरश्रेष्ठ प्राणिनः कस्य नापदः। संस्पृशन्त्यग्निवद् राजन् क्षणेन व्यपयान्ति च॥
verse.line: Take heart. Trouble touches everyone; it flares up like fire and passes.
verse.translation: Take heart, best of men. Which living being does trouble not touch? Troubles strike like fire, king, and pass in a moment.
verse.why: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.meaning: After Sita is taken, Ram is lost in grief. He returns to an empty hut and breaks down. He searches the forest and questions trees and animals. Finally he rages that he will destroy the whole world for this one loss. Lakshman steps in. He tells Ram to take heart. He asks which living being is untouched by trouble. He says trouble strikes like fire and passes in a moment.
verse.for_you: You are grieving the one you lost, and the grief feels like it will never end. Lakshman is telling Ram that trouble comes to everyone and passes. Your work and your children are still there, but the hole left behind is real. Trouble is not a sign you are weak.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing that passes, like the sun moving across the sky.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own empty hut, searching for what you lost.
asks: How do I hold on when the grief feels solid?

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Yama on the self within changing bodies.
verse.sanskrit: अशरीरँ शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् । महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
verse.line: Knowing what stays steady inside all that changes, the wise do not grieve.
verse.translation: Knowing the self as bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.
verse.why: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

prasang.title: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

verse.meaning: Yama, the god of death, speaks to Nachiketa about what does not die. He says the true self is not born, does not die, and is not killed when the body is. It is steady inside all that changes. A calm, honest life is how you find it, not cleverness or study.
verse.for_you: The grief you are drying up inside is for the body, the parent you knew. What they most were is not gone. You can hold on to the idea that what is real does not die. A quiet, honest life is enough to find it.
verse.scene_line: You are standing with death, asking what does not die.
asks: What part of me is not born and does not die?
How do I hold on to what stays steady?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse.sanskrit: चेतसा सर्वकर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः । बुद्धियोगमुपाश्रित्य मच्चित्तः सततं भव ॥
verse.line: Inwardly hand all your work to the divine, hold it as your goal, and keep your mind on it.
verse.translation: Mentally resigning all actions to me, holding me as the highest, relying on the yoga of understanding, keep your mind always on me.
verse.why: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

prasang.title: Action with devotion: surrender
prasang.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
prasang.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna at the close of their long conversation on the battlefield. Arjuna has heard much about action, knowledge, and devotion, and now Krishna tells him to gather all of it into one final movement. He says to hand over every action inwardly, to make the divine the highest aim, and to rest the mind there. The point is to reflect fully, to choose freely, and to set down the fear that comes from thinking the results belong to the self.
verse.for_you: The search you feel is not a lack of answers, but a shift in where you place your life. Your work and your care for your family are the ground you stand on. You do not need to leave them to find what you are looking for.
verse.try_today: Before you begin your work, name one task you will offer without clinging to the result.
verse.scene_line: You are at the edge of a long conversation, and the last word is a hand placed on your shoulder.
asks: How do I offer work that still needs to be done?
What does it mean to make the divine my highest aim?
Can I rest my mind while the day still demands my hands?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha, after Janaka's story, praises clear understanding (prajna).
verse.sanskrit: य एव यत्नः क्रियते बाह्यार्थोपार्जने जनैः । स एव यत्नः कर्तव्यः पूर्वं प्रज्ञाविवर्धने ॥
verse.line: Put the effort you spend earning money into growing wiser first.
verse.translation: The very effort people put into earning outer wealth should first be put into growing wisdom.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Rama after telling the story of King Janaka. Janaka had heard sages singing about the true self in his garden. He climbed to his palace roof, shaken, and questioned everything he had lived for. Then his doorkeeper called him to his daily duties. He chose not to run away. He got up and did his work, but with a mind that no longer clung to the results.
verse.for_you: You are still doing the work, but the mind is tired of the old reasons. The effort you put into earning a living can also be the effort that grows your understanding. The same hands that manage the house and the job can hold a steadier view.
verse.try_today: When you start the next task, notice the difference between doing it and needing it to prove something.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the roof's edge, hearing the doorkeeper call you back to your duties.
asks: How do I know if my mind is truly free?
Can I find peace without leaving my life?

story.title: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
story.story_hook: Satyakama wanted to study, but first he had to ask his mother a question she could not answer.
story.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
story.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

anchor.speaker: Satyakama
anchor.setting: Satyakama returns, taught along the way by a bull, fire, a swan and a diver bird.
anchor.sanskrit: ब्रह्मविदिव वै सोम्य भासि को नु त्वानुशशासेत्यन्ये मनुष्येभ्य इति ह प्रतिजज्ञे भगवाꣳस्त्वेव मे कामे ब्रूयात् ॥ श्रुतꣳह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्य आचार्याद्धैव विद्या विदिता साधिष्ठं प्रापतीति तस्मै हैतदेवोवाचात्र ह न किंचन वीयायेति वीयायेति ॥
anchor.line: Though nature had taught him, he still asked his teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher goes deepest.
anchor.translation: 'You shine like one who knows Brahman, dear one. Who has taught you?' 'Others than men,' he admitted. 'But I wish that you, sir, would teach me, for I have heard from people like you that knowledge learned from a teacher best reaches its goal.' So the teacher taught him that very knowledge, and nothing was left out.
anchor.why: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

story.hook_title: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.teaser: A boy didn't know who his father was, and told his teacher the truth anyway
story.for_you: Satyakama went to his teacher with nothing but the truth about where he came from. You are looking for a deeper ground to stand on, and the first step is admitting you do not have all the answers yet. Let your children see you searching honestly rather than performing certainty.
asks: How do I tell my children about my own searching?
What if I never find the solid ground I am looking for?
Is it okay to not know where I come from?

understanding.emotion: i'm looking for something deeper to lean on
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call searching for what it's all for, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.insight: Nothing is exactly wrong, and that's the hard part. You've outgrown the reasons that used to carry you.
understanding.mechanism_label: Searching for what it's all for

situations.label: I want to reconnect with my roots
Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

queries.hook: The wish to understand what these texts teach, and to find in them something steady to lean on.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: What passes cannot fill the heart; turning toward what lasts gives each day a quiet purpose.
queries.act: Turn toward what lasts: serve, study, reflect daily, and offer your work to something beyond yourself.
queries.story: A story of a student who came to a teacher with questions and was led, step by step, toward the truth.

understanding.life_context: Working and raising kids. Feels searching; closest to "I lost a parent" and afraid of death".

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
verse.sanskrit: गुणैः संवेष्टितो देहस्तिष्ठत्यायाति याति च । आत्मा न गन्ता नागन्ता किमेनमनुशोचसि ॥
verse.line: The body comes and goes; what you truly are does not. Why grieve so?
verse.translation: The body, made of nature's qualities, comes, stays and goes. The Self neither comes nor goes. Why grieve for it?
verse.why: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.
verse.misuse: Grief is natural; this offers perspective, not a rule against mourning.

prasang.title: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

verse.meaning: Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka. Janaka sits before him, caught in the roles of king and doer. Ashtavakra tells him the body is born of nature and it will leave. The Self is the ocean. It does not come and it does not go. The waves of life rise and fall, but the ocean remains. The teaching asks us to rest in what does not change and let the waves of life move without losing ourselves.
verse.for_you: You are sitting in a life full of weight, the work and the children, and the loss of your parent has left you looking for something that will not leave. The verse reminds you that you are not the body that was lost, nor the roles you play.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment where you feel the weight of the loss, and let it pass through you like a wave.
verse.scene_line: You are the king before the sage, caught between the role and the truth.
asks: How do I rest when the body is all I know?
Can I let the loss go without letting go of love?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: On the joy at the heart of things.
verse.sanskrit: यद्वै तत् सुकृतम् रसो वै सः रसꣳह्येवायं लब्ध्वाऽऽनन्दी भवति ।
verse.line: It is the very flavour of life. Whoever tastes it is filled with joy.
verse.translation: That which is well made is the essence itself. Having found that essence, a person becomes joyful.
verse.why: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

matched.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful

prasang.title: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

verse.meaning: A teacher speaks to students in a quiet place. They are trying to understand what joy is and where it lives. The teacher says that the very best thing in life is its own true nature. Once you find that true nature, you become full of joy. You do not need to earn it or make it happen. It is already there. When you know it, you are free from fear and from feeling bad about the past.
verse.for_you: You are looking for something to hold onto after losing a parent, and you are afraid of what comes after. You have been looking outside yourself, in your work, in your family, for an answer. This teaching says the answer is not a thing to find.
verse.try_today: Notice one small moment of simple pleasure today.
verse.scene_line: You are sitting in your own quiet room, tasting the truth of your own life.
asks: How do I find this joy when my mind is full of work and worry?
How do I stop searching and start tasting?

verse.speaker: Ashtavakra
verse.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
verse.sanskrit: स्वाराज्ये भैक्षवृत्तौ च लाभालाभे जने वने । निर्विकल्पस्वभावस्य न विशेषोऽस्ति योगिनः ॥
verse.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
verse.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.

words.en: of the one with undoubting nature

verse.why: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

prasang.title: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

verse.meaning: In the closing verses of the text, the sage Ashtavakra speaks to Janaka. Janaka has heard much, and now Ashtavakra sums up the nature of a mind that is at rest. He tells him that for a person whose nature is steady, the seat of a king and the bowl of a beggar look the same. Gain and loss, the noise of a crowd and the silence of the forest, they do not move him. The teaching is simple. Peace is not a place you reach or a feeling you chase.
verse.for_you: The life you carry right now, with its work and its children and its own small moments, is the very place where this steadiness is meant to live. You are not looking for a new room or a new job to feel at peace.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment of ordinary life today, and let it be exactly as it is without trying to change it.

verse.speaker: Yama
verse.setting: Yama on the inner self and the world's pain.
verse.sanskrit: सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः । एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ॥
verse.line: The sun shows every flaw yet stays untouched. Your deepest self stays untouched by the world's sorrow.
verse.translation: Just as the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the flaws the eyes see outside, so the one inner self of all beings is not stained by the sorrow of the world; it stands apart.
verse.why: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

prasang.title: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

verse.meaning: Yama is speaking to Nachiketa, who has been asking what happens after death. Yama wants to show him where to look for what lasts. He tells him to turn the gaze inward. Our senses always look outward, so we miss what is inside. The wise person stops searching among passing things and looks within instead. When the knots in the heart are cut, a person is free.
verse.for_you: You are looking for something deeper to hold onto after losing a parent. The grief is real, but it is not the whole of you. What stays is not out there among passing things. It is the part of you that remains when the body and the roles change.
verse.try_today: Notice the part of you that stays when the noise of the day stops.
verse.scene_line: You are turning your gaze inward, away from the passing world.
asks: How do I know what is inside and what is just passing feeling?
Can the part of me that stays ever be touched by loss?

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha's closing advice to Rama on living in the world after the three vows.
verse.sanskrit: अन्तर्मुखः सन्सततं समस्तं कुर्वन्बहिष्ठं खलु कार्यजातम् । न खेदमायासि कदाचिदेव निराकृताहंकृतितामुपैषि ॥
verse.line: Stay anchored within while you do all your outer work, and you won't burn out.
verse.translation: Staying turned inward while doing all the outer work that comes to you, you will never grow weary, and you will be free of the sense of being the doer.
verse.why: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

prasang.title: Shiva's three vows: be a great doer, enjoyer and letter-go
prasang.summary: Vasishtha gives Rama three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi: be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer. A great doer acts fully and on time without clinging; a great enjoyer takes in joys and sorrows evenly, like the ocean takes in rivers; a great renouncer lets go inside. Live this way and work won't wear you out.
prasang.lesson: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha speaks to Rama after he has taken his vows to live in the world. He tells him to keep his attention turned inward even while he does all the outer work that comes to him. This means you can act fully and take in everything life gives you without wearing yourself out. The outside world moves and changes, but your inner place stays steady. By staying anchored inside, you do your part without carrying the weight of being the one who has to make it all happen.
verse.for_you: You are holding the weight of the house, the office, and the people who need you, and the searching has made that weight feel heavier than it is. The texts call this the outer work that comes to you, and they say you can do it all without burning out.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own outer work, anchored inside.
asks: How do I let go inside while the house still needs me?
Can I enjoy the work without getting tired of it?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna opens the teaching on knowing him fully.
verse.sanskrit: श्री भगवानुवाचमय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः । असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु ॥
verse.line: Keep your mind attached to me, lean on me, keep practising. You will come to know me fully.
verse.translation: Hear, Partha, how with your mind attached to me, practising yoga and taking refuge in me, you will know me fully, without doubt.

matched.label: I want to reconnect with my roots

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, right before the great war. He is telling Arjuna that the way to know him completely is to keep the mind fixed on him. This means to stay attached, to lean in, to keep practicing. It is a steady, repeated action. The verse proposes that knowing the deepest reality is not a single insight, but a continuous practice of keeping the mind on what is real.
verse.for_you: You are doing the outer work of your life and the inner work of your grief at the same time. The verse suggests that the path forward is not to stop the outer work, but to keep the mind attached to the one constant.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when your mind rests on what stays, not on what passes.
verse.scene_line: You are on the field of your own life, and the teaching is to keep the mind fixed on what endures.
asks: How do I keep my mind attached when my thoughts scatter?
What does it mean to practice attachment in the middle of my day?
Is this a feeling I have to create, or a choice I make?

story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

anchor.speaker: Janaka
anchor.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
anchor.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
anchor.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
anchor.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
anchor.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
anchor.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

story.hook_title: King Janaka overheard a song in his garden that he couldn't stop thinking about
story.teaser: King Janaka overheard a song in his garden that he couldn't stop thinking about
story.for_you: King Janaka heard a song that shook his certainty about his throne. He did not abandon his garden or his doorkeeper. He simply stopped clutching. You are not asked to leave your work or your grief behind.
asks: How do I work without clutching the result?
Can my mind stay free while I care for others?
